title: Lost Field Notebooks Unlock 55-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fish Mystery
summary:
Field notebooks recently recovered from a late paleontologist have provided the crucial missing details researchers needed to complete a study of a remarkable fossil fish discovered nearly three decades ago. The story began in 1999 when Dr. Richard Köhler uncovered the fossil during an expedition to Pitt Island in the Chatham Islands, New Zealand. While exploring the western coastline above Waihere Bay, Köhler spotted a three-dimensionally preserved, mummified fish fossil embedded in a steep cliff. To recover it, he walked 3 km back to his lodging in Flowerpot Bay to borrow a ladder, then carefully extracted the fossil in several large, heavy blocks.

Back at the University of Otago, Emeritus Professor Daphne Lee and the late Professor Ewan Fordyce recognized its significance. The fossil was painstakingly prepared by the late fossil preparator Andrew Grebneff. Eventually, fossil fish specialist Professor Mike Gottfried from Michigan State University began investigating. Researchers determined the 1.2-meter-long mummified fish was a tarpon, a species no longer found in New Zealand waters. Modern tarpon are large predatory fish that swallow smaller fish whole. Its anatomy—elongated body, thick rigid scales, powerful tail fin, and large upward-facing mouth—suggests it was an active top predator.

Despite the fossil's importance, critical geological information about the exact discovery site was missing, and Köhler had passed away. By the time Ewan died in November 2023, a draft paper was ready but couldn't be finished without the location data. The breakthrough came in early 2025 when one of Köhler's children, studying at Otago, visited the department and donated his father's field notebooks, including those from the Pitt Island expedition. This allowed researchers to prepare a Fossil Record Form and scientifically catalogue the fossil. The study, published in the New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, represents the first report of a high-in-the-food-chain predatory bony fish from the Paleogene period (about 55 million years ago) in New Zealand.
why_it_matters: This story shows that science is not just about brains in a lab — it depends on careful record‑keeping and sometimes on luck and generosity across generations. Understanding past ocean predators also helps us predict how marine ecosystems might shift as the climate changes today.

background_read: The Chatham Islands, located about 800 km east of mainland New Zealand, are known for their rich fossil deposits from the Paleogene period — a time when Earth's climate was much warmer, and marine life was recovering and diversifying after the dinosaurs went extinct.

Tarpons today are found in warmer waters like the Atlantic and Indo‑Pacific oceans, but they are absent from modern New Zealand; finding a fossil tarpon there shows how ocean conditions and fish distributions have changed dramatically over millions of years.

Field notebooks are often the most important tool a paleontologist carries, because the exact layer and location of a fossil provide essential context — without them, a specimen's scientific value drops sharply, as this story demonstrates.
The late Ewan Fordyce was a prominent paleontologist at the University of Otago, New Zealand, who mentored many students and left a legacy of research on ancient marine mammals and fishes.

perspectives.description: The eventual recovery of the notebooks highlights the dedication of scientists who prepare specimens and collect data for decades, and the role of families in preserving scientific heritage. The published study now adds a significant top predator to New Zealand's ancient marine record.

The long delay and near‑loss reveal a weakness in how field data is archived and shared. If Köhler's family had not kept the notebooks, or if they had been destroyed, an important piece of natural history would have remained unknown — raising questions about data management standards in science.

This case is a classic example of how paleontology often pieces together evidence from fragmented sources — fossils, notebooks, memories — and how scientific timelines can span decades. It also underscores the importance of institutional knowledge passed through university departments like Otago's.

More legacy field notebooks could still exist in attics and offices; digitizing such records would prevent future bottlenecks. The discovery also encourages renewed fossil hunting in the Chatham Islands, where other unexpected Paleogene species may await.
